prompt: What is the solvent in a solution?

choices.text: The major component of the solution
The minor component of the solution
choices.why: The minor component is the solute. The solvent is the major component.

choices.text: Always water
choices.why: Water is a common solvent, but not the only one. Air, for example, is a solution whose solvent is N2.

choices.text: Always the liquid component
choices.why: Solutions exist for every phase. In air both the solute (O2) and the solvent (N2) are gases.

explanation: The major component of a solution is called the solvent, and the minor component is called the solute.

prompt: When identifying the solvent and the solute, what do "major" and "minor" refer to?

choices.text: Which component has the greater or lesser presence by mass or by moles
Which component was added to the container first
choices.why: The order of mixing doesn't matter. The solvent is whichever component is present in the greater amount.

choices.text: Which component has the higher boiling point
choices.why: Boiling point doesn't decide it. Major and minor refer to the amount of each component, by mass or by moles.

choices.text: Which component is a liquid
choices.why: Solvents can be gases or solids too. Major and minor refer to amounts, by mass or by moles.

explanation: "Major" and "minor" indicate which component has the greater or lesser presence by mass or moles. The major component is the solvent; the minor one is the solute.

prompt: A solution is made by dissolving 5.0 g of potassium nitrate, KNO3, in 250 g of water. Which is the solute?

choices.text: KNO3
Water
choices.why: Water is the major component, so it is the solvent.

choices.text: Both, because they are mixed together
choices.why: A solution has a solvent (the major component) and a solute (the minor component). Here the minor component is KNO3.

choices.text: Neither; a solid dissolved in a liquid isn't a solution
choices.why: Salt water is a solution of a solid in a liquid. Solutions exist for every possible phase of solute and solvent.

explanation: KNO3 (5.0 g) is the minor component, so it is the solute; water (250 g) is the major component, so it is the solvent.

prompt: Soda water is a solution of carbon dioxide gas in liquid water. Which is the solute?

choices.text: CO2
Water
choices.why: Water is the major component, so it is the solvent.

choices.text: Nothing; a gas can't be a solute
choices.why: Solutes can be in any phase. In soda water the solute is gaseous CO2.

choices.text: The bubbles that escape when the bottle is opened
choices.why: The bubbles are CO2 leaving the solution. The solute is the CO2 dissolved in the water.

explanation: Soda water is a solution of gaseous CO2 (the minor component, the solute) in liquid water (the major component, the solvent).

prompt: Air can be thought of as a solution of O2 in N2. Which component is the solvent?

choices.text: N2, because it is the major component
O2, because it is the gas we breathe
choices.why: Which gas matters most to us doesn't decide it. O2 is the minor component, so it is the solute.

choices.text: Neither; a mixture of gases has no solvent
choices.why: Solutions exist for every phase, including gas in gas. The major gas, N2, is the solvent.

choices.text: Whichever gas is heavier
choices.why: The solvent is the component present in the greater amount, here N2.

explanation: Air is a solution of a gaseous solute (O2) in a gaseous solvent (N2). The solvent is the major component.

prompt: A small amount of a solid is dissolved in a large amount of liquid ethanol. What is the phase of the resulting solution?

choices.text: Liquid, the same phase as the solvent
Solid, the same phase as the solute
choices.why: The overall phase of a solution is the phase of the solvent, not the solute.

choices.text: Partly solid and partly liquid
choices.why: Once the solid dissolves, the solution is a single phase: that of the solvent.

choices.text: Gas, because dissolving releases the particles
choices.why: Dissolving doesn't turn the solution into a gas. A solution has the same phase as its solvent.

explanation: In all cases, the overall phase of a solution is the same phase as the solvent. Ethanol, the solvent here, is a liquid.

prompt: Which pair of terms describes concentration only qualitatively?

choices.text: Dilute and concentrated
Molarity and molality
choices.why: These are quantitative units: they give an exact amount of solute per amount of solution or solvent.

choices.text: Mass percentage and parts per million
choices.why: These are quantitative: they give an exact ratio of masses.

choices.text: Grams and liters
choices.why: These are units of mass and volume, not descriptions of concentration.

explanation: Dilute describes a solution with very little solute and concentrated one with a lot of solute. These terms are qualitative: they describe more or less, but not exactly how much.

prompt: What is the solubility of a solute?

choices.text: The maximum amount of it that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent
The amount of it that is dissolved in a particular solution
choices.why: That is the concentration of one solution. Solubility is the most that can dissolve.

choices.text: How quickly it dissolves
choices.why: Solubility is about how much can dissolve, not how fast.

choices.text: Any amount that can dissolve in exactly 1 L of solution
choices.why: Solubility is the maximum amount, usually given per 100 g of solvent at a stated temperature.

explanation: In most cases only a certain maximum amount of solute can dissolve in a given amount of solvent. That maximum is the solubility, usually expressed as the amount that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature.

prompt: At 25°C, the solubilities in grams per 100 g of water are: CaCO3, 0.0006; NaCl, 36.1; KBr, 70.7; NaNO3, 94.6. Which compound is the most soluble?

choices.text: NaNO3
KBr
choices.why: KBr is very soluble (70.7 g), but NaNO3 is more so (94.6 g).

choices.text: NaCl
choices.why: NaCl dissolves up to 36.1 g per 100 g of water, much less than NaNO3.

choices.text: CaCO3
choices.why: CaCO3 is the least soluble of the four, at only 0.0006 g per 100 g of water.

explanation: The largest solubility is the one with the most grams per 100 g of water: NaNO3, at 94.6 g.

prompt: The solubility of KBr is 70.7 g per 100 g of H2O at 25°C. What is the maximum mass of KBr, in grams, that can dissolve in 200.0 g of water at 25°C?
explanation: Twice as much water dissolves twice as much solute: 200.0 g H2O × (70.7 g KBr / 100 g H2O) = 141 g KBr.

prompt: The solubility of NaNO3 is 94.6 g per 100 g of H2O at 25°C. What is the maximum mass of NaNO3, in grams, that can dissolve in 50.0 g of water at 25°C?
The solubility of NaCl is 36.1 g per 100 g of H2O at 25°C. If 50.0 g of NaCl is stirred into 100.0 g of water at 25°C, how many grams of NaCl remain undissolved?
explanation: Only 36.1 g can dissolve in 100 g of water, so 50.0 g − 36.1 g = 13.9 g stays undissolved, and the solution is saturated.

prompt: The solubility of KBr is 70.7 g per 100 g of H2O at 25°C. A solution contains 40.0 g of KBr in 100.0 g of water at 25°C. How many more grams of KBr can dissolve before the solution is saturated?
explanation: The maximum is 70.7 g, so 70.7 g − 40.0 g = 30.7 g more can dissolve.

prompt: The solubility of NaCl is 36.1 g per 100 g of H2O at 25°C. What is the minimum mass of water, in grams, needed to dissolve 9.00 g of NaCl at 25°C?
explanation: Use the solubility the other way up: 9.00 g NaCl × (100 g H2O / 36.1 g NaCl) = 24.9 g H2O.

prompt: At 25°C, 36.1 g of NaCl can dissolve in 100 g of water, but only 0.00019 g of AgCl can. How many times more NaCl than AgCl, by mass, can dissolve in the same amount of water?
explanation: 36.1 g ÷ 0.00019 g = 1.9 × 10^5. Solubilities vary widely, even among simple ionic compounds.

prompt: The solubility of NaCl is 36.1 g per 100 g of H2O at 25°C. A solution contains 20.0 g of NaCl dissolved in 100 g of water at 25°C. How is it described?

choices.text: Unsaturated
Saturated
choices.why: A saturated solution holds the maximum, 36.1 g. This one holds only 20.0 g, so more could dissolve.

choices.text: Supersaturated
choices.why: A supersaturated solution holds more than the maximum. 20.0 g is less than 36.1 g.

choices.text: Insoluble
choices.why: Insoluble describes a substance that barely dissolves; NaCl is quite soluble in water.

explanation: When less than the maximum amount of solute is dissolved, the solution is unsaturated. 20.0 g is below NaCl's solubility of 36.1 g per 100 g of water.

prompt: What does it mean for a solution to be saturated?

choices.text: The maximum amount of solute has been dissolved in the given amount of solvent.
The solution contains a lot of solute.
choices.why: That describes a concentrated solution. A saturated solution can be very dilute if the solute's solubility is small.

choices.text: More than the maximum amount of solute has been dissolved.
choices.why: That describes a supersaturated solution.

choices.text: The solute and solvent are present in equal amounts.
choices.why: Saturation depends on the solute's solubility, not on equal amounts.

explanation: When the maximum amount of solute has been dissolved in a given amount of solvent, the solution is saturated with solute.

prompt: A solution contains 0.00019 g of AgCl in 100 g of water at 25°C, the most AgCl that can dissolve. Which description fits it best?

choices.text: Saturated and dilute
Saturated and concentrated
choices.why: It is saturated, but with so little solute dissolved it is dilute. Saturated doesn't mean concentrated.

choices.text: Unsaturated and dilute
choices.why: It holds the maximum amount of AgCl that can dissolve, so it is saturated.

choices.text: Supersaturated
choices.why: It holds exactly the maximum, not more than the maximum.

explanation: Saturated and unsaturated are qualitative terms because each solute has its own solubility. A saturated AgCl solution has so little solute that it is also rather dilute, while a saturated NaCl solution (36.1 g per 100 g) is rather concentrated.

prompt: A student dissolves 36.1 g of NaCl in 100 g of water at 25°C, where NaCl's solubility is 36.1 g per 100 g, and calls the solution supersaturated because it holds so much salt. What is wrong?

choices.text: It holds exactly the maximum amount, so it is saturated; a supersaturated solution holds more than the maximum.
It is unsaturated, because some more NaCl could still dissolve.
choices.why: 36.1 g is the most that can dissolve in 100 g of water at 25°C, so no more can dissolve: the solution is saturated.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; any concentrated solution is supersaturated.
choices.why: Supersaturated has a specific meaning: more than the maximum amount of solute is dissolved.

choices.text: It is dilute, because 36.1 g is less than 100 g.
choices.why: 36.1 g of NaCl in 100 g of water is a lot of solute; the solution is rather concentrated, and saturated.

explanation: A solution holding exactly the maximum amount of solute is saturated. A supersaturated solution holds more than the maximum, which usually takes heating the solvent and cooling the solution slowly.

prompt: How is a supersaturated solution usually made?

choices.text: By heating the solvent, dissolving more solute than normally dissolves, and letting the solution cool slowly and carefully
By adding solute to a saturated solution and stirring hard
choices.why: Extra solute added to a saturated solution at the same temperature just stays undissolved.

choices.text: By adding more solvent to a saturated solution
choices.why: Adding solvent makes the solution unsaturated, not supersaturated.

choices.text: By dropping a crystal of solute into the solution
choices.why: Adding a crystal is what makes the excess solute precipitate from a supersaturated solution.

explanation: It is sometimes possible to dissolve more than the maximum amount of solute, usually by heating the solvent, dissolving more solute than would normally dissolve, and letting the solution cool slowly and carefully.

prompt: A single crystal of solute is dropped into a supersaturated solution. What happens?

choices.text: The excess solute precipitates from the solution.
The crystal dissolves, and the solution becomes even more concentrated.
choices.why: A supersaturated solution already holds more than the maximum. It can't dissolve more; instead, the excess comes out.

choices.text: Nothing happens, because supersaturated solutions are stable.
choices.why: Supersaturated solutions are not stable; given an opportunity, the excess solute precipitates.

choices.text: The solvent evaporates.
choices.why: The crystal gives the excess solute a place to come out of solution; the solvent doesn't evaporate.

explanation: Supersaturated solutions are not stable. Given an opportunity, such as a crystal of solute dropped in, the excess solute precipitates from the solution.

prompt: What does the rule "like dissolves like" say?

choices.text: A solute is likely to dissolve in a solvent whose molecules experience the same intermolecular forces.
A solute dissolves only in a solvent with the same chemical formula.
choices.why: "Like" refers to the kinds of intermolecular forces, not to identical substances.

choices.text: Solids dissolve only in solids, and liquids only in liquids.
choices.why: Solutions exist for every combination of phases, such as solid NaCl in liquid water.

choices.text: A solute dissolves in a solvent with the same molar mass.
choices.why: Molar mass isn't the deciding factor. The rule is about matching intermolecular forces.

explanation: If molecules of a solute experience the same intermolecular forces as the solvent, the solute will likely dissolve in that solvent. This is a general rule, not an absolute statement, so it must be applied with care.

prompt: Why does NaCl dissolve in water but not in vegetable oil?

choices.text: NaCl, made of ions, is very polar; water is very polar, and oil is generally nonpolar.
Oil is too thick for the salt crystals to move through.
choices.why: Thickness isn't the reason. Polar NaCl doesn't share the intermolecular forces of nonpolar oil.

choices.text: NaCl reacts chemically with water but not with oil.
choices.why: Dissolving NaCl in water is not a reaction that makes new substances; the ions just separate and mix with the water.

choices.text: Water is nonpolar, like NaCl, and oil is polar.
choices.why: It's the reverse: water is very polar, and so is NaCl, while oil is generally nonpolar.

explanation: NaCl is a very polar substance because it is composed of ions, so it dissolves in very polar water but not in oil, which is generally nonpolar: like dissolves like.

prompt: Beeswax dissolves in liquid hexane but not in water. What does this tell you?

choices.text: Beeswax and hexane are both nonpolar, while water is polar.
Beeswax and water are both polar.
choices.why: If they were both polar, the wax would be expected to dissolve in the water.

choices.text: Hexane is an ionic compound.
choices.why: Hexane is a nonpolar hydrocarbon. Nonpolar wax dissolves in it for that reason.

choices.text: Beeswax dissolves in anything except water.
choices.why: Wax dissolves in solvents like itself, nonpolar ones. Polar solvents generally won't dissolve it.

explanation: Nonpolar wax dissolves in nonpolar hexane but not in polar water: like dissolves like.

prompt: Hexane, C6H14, is a nonpolar solvent. Which substance would you expect to dissolve better in hexane?

choices.text: Br2
KBr
choices.why: KBr is ionic and so very polar; it would be expected to dissolve in polar water, not nonpolar hexane.

choices.text: They would dissolve equally well, because both contain bromine.
choices.why: What matters is the intermolecular forces. Br2 is nonpolar, like hexane; KBr is made of ions.

choices.text: Neither; nothing dissolves in hexane.
choices.why: Nonpolar substances, like wax and Br2, dissolve in nonpolar hexane.

explanation: Br2 is a nonpolar molecule, like hexane, so it is expected to dissolve in hexane. KBr is ionic, so it dissolves in polar solvents like water instead.

prompt: Which substance would you expect to be more soluble in water: methanol, CH3OH, or octane, C8H18?

choices.text: Methanol, because like water it experiences hydrogen bonding
Octane, because it is a larger molecule
choices.why: Size doesn't make a substance dissolve in water. Octane is nonpolar, unlike water.

choices.text: Octane, because it contains hydrogen atoms
choices.why: Octane's H atoms are bonded to C, so it has no hydrogen bonding and is nonpolar.

choices.text: Neither; molecular compounds don't dissolve in water
choices.why: Many molecular compounds dissolve in water, like sugar and methanol. What matters is the intermolecular forces.

explanation: Methanol has an O–H bond, so it experiences hydrogen bonding, as water does. Octane is a nonpolar hydrocarbon. Like dissolves like, so methanol is more soluble in water.

prompt: Ethanol, C2H5OH, mixes with water in any proportion. Which explanation fits the "like dissolves like" rule?

choices.text: Both ethanol and water experience hydrogen bonding.
Both ethanol and water are ionic compounds.
choices.why: Neither is ionic; both are covalent molecules. They share hydrogen bonding through their O–H bonds.

choices.text: Ethanol is nonpolar, and nonpolar substances dissolve in everything.
choices.why: Ethanol has a polar O–H bond and hydrogen bonding. Nonpolar substances generally don't dissolve in water.

choices.text: Both are liquids, and all liquids mix.
choices.why: Not all liquids mix: oil and water don't. Ethanol and water mix because they share the same intermolecular forces.

explanation: Ethanol has an H atom bonded to O, so it experiences hydrogen bonding, just as water does. Their molecules attract each other through the same intermolecular forces, so ethanol dissolves in water.

prompt: How should the "like dissolves like" rule be used?

choices.text: As a general rule for predicting solubility, applied with care because it is not an absolute statement
As an absolute law with no exceptions
choices.why: The section stresses that it is a general rule, not an absolute statement.

choices.text: Only for ionic compounds
choices.why: It applies to molecular solutes too, such as wax in hexane.

choices.text: Only to calculate exact solubilities
choices.why: The rule predicts whether a solute is likely to dissolve, not how many grams will dissolve.

explanation: "Like dissolves like" is a general rule for predicting whether a solute is soluble in a given solvent. It is not an absolute statement, so it must be applied with care.

prompt: Why are "saturated" and "unsaturated" also qualitative terms, even though saturation is defined by a maximum amount?

choices.text: Each solute has its own solubility, so knowing a solution is saturated doesn't tell you how much solute it contains.
Because saturation can't be measured.
choices.why: Solubilities can be measured and tabulated. The point is that "saturated" alone doesn't give an amount.

choices.text: Because every saturated solution has the same concentration.
choices.why: Saturated solutions vary hugely: saturated AgCl is very dilute, while saturated NaCl is quite concentrated.

choices.text: Because they describe the color of the solution.
choices.why: They describe whether more solute could dissolve, not color.

explanation: Saturated and unsaturated are qualitative because each solute has its own solubility. A saturated AgCl solution is rather dilute, while a saturated NaCl solution is rather concentrated, so more precise units are needed.
